# Anxiety disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Psychiatric disorders > Anxiety disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/kP0mUT)

---

## Summary

Anxiety disorders cover a broad spectrum of conditions characterized by excessive and persistent fear (an emotional response to real or perceived imminent threats), anxiety (the anticipation of a future threat), worry (apprehensive expectation), and/or avoidance behavior. The etiology of anxiety disorders is multifactorial and may involve genetic, developmental, environmental, and psychosocial factors. Therapy typically consists of a combination of pharmacotherapy, especially <u>selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors</u> (<u>SSRIs</u>), and <u>psychotherapy</u>, especially <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> (<u>CBT</u>).

---

## Overview

### Description




* Excessive and persistent fear (an emotional response to real or perceived imminent threats), anxiety (the anticipation of a future threat), worry (apprehensive expectation), and/or avoidance behavior

* Physical manifestations that are disproportionate to the real magnitude of the trigger

* Anxiety disorders include <u>generalized anxiety disorder</u>, <u>panic disorder</u>, <u>specific phobias</u>, and <u>selective mutism</u>.





### Comparison of anxiety disorders




| Overview of the most important anxiety disorders |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Characteristics | <u>Generalized anxiety disorder</u> (<u>GAD</u>) | <u>Panic disorder</u> | <u>Social anxiety disorder</u> | <u>Specific phobias</u> | <u>Agoraphobia</u> | <u>Substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder</u> |
| Clinical features | <br>* Excessive and persistent anxiety and/or fear<br><br> | <br>* Recurrent unexpected <u>panic attacks</u><br><br> | <br>* Pronounced fear and/or anxiety of social situations that involve scrutiny from others<br><br> | <br>* Persistent and intense fears of particular situations or objects<br><br> | <br>* Pronounced fear or anxiety of situations that are perceived as difficult to <u>escape</u> from<br><br> | <br>* Prominent anxiety or <u>panic attacks</u> after using or stopping a substance/medication<br><br> |
| Triggers | <br>* No definitive trigger or source<br><br> | <br>* May not have an obvious trigger<br><br> | <br>* Social interaction and/or performance of any actions in public<br><br> | <br>* One or more specific situations or objects<br><br> | <br><br>* Being in enclosed spaces or open public spaces<br><br>* Crowds<br><br>* Being alone<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Alcohol</u><br><br>* <u>Caffeine</u><br><br>* <u>Corticosteroids</u><br><br>* <u>Amphetamines</u>, <u>cannabis</u><br><br><br> |
| Duration of symptoms required for diagnosis | <br>* ≥ 6 months<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Panic attacks</u>: several minutes<br><br>* Fear of subsequent attacks: ≥ 1 month<br><br><br> | <br>* ≥ 6 months<br><br> | <br>* ≥ 6 months<br><br> | <br>* ≥ 6 months in ≥ 2 different situations<br><br> | <br>* Within 1 month of using or stopping the substance/medication<br><br> |
| Treatment of anxiety disorders | <br><br>* First line: <u>SSRIs</u> or <u>SNRIs</u> and/or <u>CBT</u><br><br>* Alternatives: <u>buspirone</u>, applied relaxation therapy, <u>biofeedback</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Acute <u>panic attack</u>: short-acting <u>benzodiazepines</u> (e.g. <u>alprazolam</u>)<br><br>* Long-term management: <u>SSRIs</u> or <u>SNRIs</u> and/or <u>CBT</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>SSRIs</u> or <u>SNRIs</u> and/or <u>CBT</u><br><br>* <u>Performance-only social anxiety disorder</u>: <u>CBT</u> and/or <u>propranolol</u> or <u>clonazepam</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>CBT</u> (desensitization therapy)<br><br>* <u>Benzodiazepine</u> or <u>SSRIs</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>CBT</u><br><br>* <u>SSRIs</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Discontinuation of the substance/medication<br><br>* <u>CBT</u><br><br>* <u>SSRIs</u> or <u>SNRIs</u><br><br><br> |

## Etiology

* Neurobiological and genetic factors

* Disruption of the <u>serotonin</u> system

* Dysfunction of <u>GABA</u> inhibitory transmission

* Environmental, developmental, and psychosocial factors

* <u>Stress</u>

* Smoking (<u>risk factor</u> for <u>panic disorder</u> and <u>panic attacks</u>)

* Psychological trauma, especially during childhood

* Substance use in <u>substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder</u>

* <u>Anxiety due to another medical condition</u> (e.g., <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>asthma</u>)

---

## Generalized anxiety disorder

### Definition




* An anxiety disorder characterized by excessive and persistent anxiety for ≥ 6 months

* Symptoms can be triggered in various situations, with or without an identifiable <u>stressor</u>, and cause significant social or occupational dysfunction.





### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[1]](/library/K8WUnM0)




* Lifetime <u>prevalence</u>: 4–7% [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)

* Typically adult onset  [[1]](/library/K8WUnM0)

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2:1) [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)





### Clinical features [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)




* Prolonged, excessive, pervasive worrying and anxiety

* Nervousness, restlessness

* Irritability

* Muscle tension

* <u>Somnolence</u>, fatigue

* Concentration difficulties

* <u>Insomnia</u>

* Medically unexplained physical symptoms (e.g., <u>chest pain</u>, racing <u>heart</u>)





### Screening [[4]](/library/pG1LZi0)[[5]](/library/FlWgAl0)




* Indicated for all individuals aged 8–64 years.  [[4]](/library/pG1LZi0)[[5]](/library/FlWgAl0)

* Screening tools include:

* Adults: <u>GAD-2</u> , <u>GAD-7</u>

* Postpartum individuals: <u>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale</u> (<u>EPDS</u>) anxiety subscale   [[6]](/library/68WjnM0)

* Children and <u>adolescents</u>: <u>Patient Health Questionnaire for Adolescents</u>, Screen for Child Anxiety Related Disorders [[4]](/library/pG1LZi0)[[7]](/library/p8WLnM0)[[8]](/library/J8WsnM0)





![GAD-2 anxiety scale](media/oo09g9lyqo3bj228epiglmlg.jpg)

GAD-2 anxiety scale

![GAD-7 anxiety scale](media/jnmizxrh8blu41o87b9zd603.jpg)

GAD-7 anxiety scale

![Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale](media/f6162zxq5dtpturxl750cyst.jpg)

Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale




### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)[[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)




#### Approach




* Consider <u>GAD</u> in those with a positive screening or who express pervasive worrying, anxiety, and/or medically unexplained physical symptoms.

* Perform a complete <u>patient history</u> and <u>physical examination</u>.

* Consider diagnostic studies to rule out organic causes.

* Confirm the diagnosis using the <u>DSM-5</u> criteria for <u>GAD</u>.

* Assess for psychiatric and medical comorbidities, including <u>substance use disorder</u>.

* <u>Evaluate suicide risk</u>.

* Consult <u>psychiatry</u> if there is diagnostic uncertainty or concern for comorbid psychiatric conditions.





> [!TIP]
> Up to 80% of individuals with <u>GAD</u> have a psychiatric comorbidity, e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u> or <u>social anxiety disorder</u>. [[1]](/library/K8WUnM0)[[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)




#### Exclusion of organic causes [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)




Consider the following studies based on clinical suspicion.




* <u>Thyroid function tests</u> to rule out <u>thyroid disease</u>

* <u>CBC</u> to rule out <u>anemia</u>

* <u>ECG</u> to rule out <u>acute coronary syndromes</u>

* <u>Urine drug screen</u> to rule out substance use or <u>poisoning</u>

* Plasma free <u>metanephrines</u> in patients with a <u>family history</u> or <u>clinical features of pheochromocytoma</u>





#### DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for GAD [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)




Diagnosis is confirmed in individuals who meet all of the following criteria.




* Excessive anxiety and worry about multiple events and/or activities (e.g., school, work) on most days for ≥ 6 months

* Worry that is difficult to control

* ≥ 3 (in adults) or ≥ 1 (in children) of the following symptoms occurring on most days over the past 6 months:

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbances

* Muscle tension

* Irritability

* Difficulty concentrating

* Fatiguing easily

* Restlessness

* Symptoms that cause significant <u>distress</u> or impairment in the professional, social, or other important areas

* Symptoms not attributable to substance use, a medical disorder (e.g., <u>pheochromocytoma</u>, <u>hyperthyroidism</u>), or other psychiatric conditions (e.g., <u>panic disorder</u>, <u>PTSD</u>, <u>somatic symptom and related disorders</u>)





### Differential diagnoses [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)




* Other anxiety disorders

* <u>Anxiety due to another medical condition</u>

* <u>Panic disorder</u>

* <u>Panic attacks</u> in <u>GAD</u> are generally precipitated by the uncontrolled escalation of anxiety and/or worry.

* <u>Panic attacks</u> in <u>panic disorder</u> are sudden and unexpected.

* <u>Social anxiety disorder</u>: Patients with <u>GAD</u> are usually comfortable in social situations and are not particularly anxious about public scrutiny.

* <u>Substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder</u>

* <u>Acute stress disorder</u>, <u>PTSD</u>

* <u>OCD</u>

* <u>Mood disorders</u>, e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u> (<u>MDD</u>), <u>bipolar disorder</u>

* Individuals with <u>GAD</u> tend to worry about the future, whereas those with <u>MDD</u> are typically anxious about the past.

* Mood swings and <u>suicidal ideation</u> are uncommon in <u>GAD</u>.

* <u>Substance withdrawal</u>, e.g., <u>alcohol</u>, <u>benzodiazepines</u>, <u>opioids</u>





### Management [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)[[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)




#### General principles




* Therapeutic options for <u>GAD</u> are <u>psychotherapy</u> and/or pharmacotherapy.

* Lifestyle modifications can help reduce and/or prevent symptoms.

* Treatment response is measured using validated tools, e.g., <u>GAD-7</u>.

* Consider indications for specialist referral, e.g., no improvement after first-line treatment.

* Consider hospitalization for patients with intractable symptoms and/or <u>suicidal ideation</u>.





> [!TIP]
> A combination of <u>psychotherapy</u> and pharmacotherapy is more effective than either treatment approach alone. [[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)




![GAD-7 anxiety scale](media/jnmizxrh8blu41o87b9zd603.jpg)

GAD-7 anxiety scale




#### <u>Psychotherapy</u>




* <u>CBT</u> (preferred)

* May include <u>exposure therapy</u>, <u>psychoeducation</u>, goal setting, relaxation, and/or <u>cognitive restructuring</u>

* Typically 12 sessions with homework [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)

* Other options include <u>supportive psychotherapy</u>, applied relaxation therapy, <u>psychodynamic therapy</u>, <u>acceptance and commitment therapy</u>, and <u>biofeedback</u>.





#### Pharmacotherapy [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)




* First-line agents 

* <u>SSRIs</u>, e.g., <u>escitalopram</u> DOSAGE, <u>paroxetine</u> DOSAGE, <u>sertraline</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)

* <u>SNRIs</u>, e.g., <u>duloxetine</u> DOSAGE, <u>venlafaxine</u> DOSAGE

* If no improvement after 8 weeks at the therapeutic dose: Switch to a different first-line agent.

* Alternative agents may be considered if there is no improvement with first-line therapy.

* <u>Buspirone</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Benzodiazepines</u> (e.g., <u>alprazolam</u>, <u>diazepam</u>) for short-term use only

* <u>Pregabalin</u>

* <u>Atypical antipsychotics</u> (e.g., <u>risperidone</u>, <u>quetiapine</u>)

* <u>Hydroxyzine</u>

* <u>TCAs</u>, e.g., <u>imipramine</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Cannabis</u> can trigger psychiatric disorders, and there is no scientific evidence to recommend its use in patients with anxiety disorders. [[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)




> [!WARNING]
> Long-term use of <u>benzodiazepines</u> is associated with significant adverse effects (e.g., motor and cognitive impairment) and risk of dependence. [[2]](/library/FFWgPM0)




> [!NOTE]
> Don't get anxious if the BUS doesn’t arrive at ONE; just take a BUSpirONE.




#### Lifestyle modifications




* <u>Sleep hygiene</u>

* Exercise

* Avoidance of <u>caffeine</u>, <u>alcohol</u>, and <u>recreational drugs</u>

* <u>Smoking cessation</u>

* <u>Mindfulness</u> (<u>meditation</u>, <u>mindfulness</u>-based <u>stress</u> reduction)





#### Indications for referral




Refer to a <u>psychiatrist</u> in any of the following situations.




* The patient has comorbid psychiatric and/or <u>substance use disorders</u>.

* There is no improvement with first-line treatment, i.e., a full course of <u>CBT</u> and/or 1–2 trials of <u>SSRI</u> or <u>SNRI</u>.

* Long-term <u>benzodiazepines</u>, <u>TCAs</u>, or <u>antipsychotics</u> are being considered.

* The patient does not tolerate pharmacotherapy.





### Special patient groups




#### Perinatal generalized anxiety disorder [[10]](/library/i8WJmM0)




* Definition: <u>GAD</u> that occurs during <u>pregnancy</u> and/or up to one year postpartum

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: ∼ 10% <u>prevalence</u> [[10]](/library/i8WJmM0)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* History of anxiety or <u>mood disorders</u>

* <u>Family history</u> of anxiety disorders

* Clinical features

* Time-consuming, overwhelming, intrusive fears about illness, mortality, and well-being of the fetus, oneself, and the other parent

* Functional impairment, such as inability to perform regular activities (in moderate to severe anxiety)

* Physical symptoms (e.g., fatigue, <u>insomnia</u>, muscle tension)

* Comorbid <u>MDD</u> (common)

* Screening: Screen all pregnant and postpartum individuals using, e.g., <u>GAD-7</u> , <u>EPDS</u> anxiety subscale  [[5]](/library/FlWgAl0)[[6]](/library/68WjnM0)[[11]](/library/S51yjh0)

* Diagnostics: Confirm diagnosis using the <u>DSM-5</u> criteria for <u>GAD</u>.

* Treatment

* Mild symptoms: <u>CBT</u> (preferred) or another type of <u>psychotherapy</u>

* Mild to moderate symptoms: <u>SSRI</u> or <u>SNRI</u>

* Moderate to severe symptoms: <u>CBT</u> and <u>SSRI</u> or <u>SNRI</u>, consider referral to <u>psychiatry</u>





![Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale](media/f6162zxq5dtpturxl750cyst.jpg)

Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale

## Acute panic attack

### Definition




An acute <u>panic attack</u> is an abrupt episode of intense fear associated with physical and cognitive symptoms. [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[13]](/library/5r1i3R0)




### Etiology [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)[[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Panic disorder</u>

* <u>Anxiety due to another medical condition</u>

* <u>Substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder</u>

* Other anxiety disorders (e.g., <u>specific phobias</u>)

* Other psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>psychotic disorders</u>)





### Clinical features [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)




Acute <u>panic attacks</u> peak within several minutes and involve ≥ 4 of the following cognitive and/or somatic symptoms:




* Cognitive symptoms

* Fear of dying

* Fear of losing control

* <u>Derealization</u> or <u>depersonalization</u>

* Somatic symptoms: overstimulation of the <u>sympathetic</u> system

* <u>Palpitations</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, or pounding <u>heart</u>

* Sweating or <u>diaphoresis</u>

* Trembling or shaking

* <u>Shortness of breath</u> or <u>smothering</u> sensation

* Choking sensation

* <u>Chest pain</u> or tightness

* Abdominal discomfort or <u>nausea</u>

* <u>Dizziness</u>, light-headedness, or faintness

* Chills or feeling hot

* <u>Paresthesias</u>





> [!NOTE]
> “STUDENTS FEAR the 3Cs:” Sweating, Trembling, Unsteadiness (<u>dizziness</u>), Derealization, Elevated <u>heart rate</u> (<u>palpitations</u>), Nausea, Tingling, and Shortness of breath; FEAR of dying or going crazy; Chest <u>pain</u>, Choking, and Chills.




### Diagnostics




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> based on typical clinical features and the exclusion of organic causes of symptoms [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[13]](/library/5r1i3R0)

* Consider basic investigations, e.g. : [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>BMP</u>

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>

* Serum and <u>urine toxicology screen</u>

* <u>ECG</u>

* Consider further targeted investigation if an underlying medical cause is suspected (see “Differential diagnosis”).





### Differential diagnoses




Consider the following based on the presenting clinical feature:




* <u>Differential diagnosis of chest pain</u>

* <u>Differential diagnosis of dyspnea</u>

* <u>Differential diagnosis of syncope and presyncope</u>

* <u>Differential diagnoses of stroke</u>

* <u>Differential diagnosis of abdominal pain</u>

* Differential diagnosis of <u>cardiac arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Differential diagnosis of sepsis</u>





### Management of acute panic attack [[14]](/library/cu1aJi0)[[15]](/library/c8YalI)




* Rule out life-threatening causes of symptoms, e.g.:

* <u>Red flags in dyspnea</u>

* <u>Red flags in chest pain</u>

* <u>Thyroid storm</u>

* Immediate interventions may include:

* Reassurance

* Deep breathing and relaxation techniques

* Short-acting <u>benzodiazepine</u> (e.g., <u>alprazolam</u>  DOSAGE) if nonpharmacological intervention fails

* See also “Acute management” in “<u>Hyperventilation syndrome</u>” and “<u>Approach to the agitated or violent patient</u>.”

* Once life-threatening causes are excluded, consider discharge to primary care or <u>psychiatry</u> for close follow-up. [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Evaluate for underlying psychiatric disorder and assess <u>suicidal risk</u>.

* See “Management” in “<u>Panic disorder</u>” for long-term treatment of recurrent <u>panic attacks</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Panic attacks</u> typically self-resolve within 30 minutes of onset and may not require acute intervention. [[14]](/library/cu1aJi0)

---

## Panic disorder

### Definition




<u>Panic disorder</u> is an anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, unexpected <u>panic attacks</u> in addition to a ≥ 1-month period of persistent worry about experiencing additional attacks or their consequences, and/or maladaptive behavior to avoid further episodes.





### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[16]](/library/irYJSq)




* Lifetime <u>prevalence</u>: 1–4% of the population [[17]](/library/8FWOPM0)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: adults aged 26–34 years [[16]](/library/irYJSq)

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2:1)





### Etiology [[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)




* Strong genetic predisposition  [[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)

* Associated conditions

* <u>Agoraphobia</u>

* <u>Substance use disorder</u>

* Comorbid <u>mood disorders</u>, e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u> (<u>MDD</u>), <u>bipolar disorder</u>





### Clinical features [[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)




* Recurrent <u>panic attacks</u> characterized by:

* Symptoms that peak within minutes

* Somatic symptoms, e.g., <u>palpitations</u>, <u>chest pain</u> or tightness, <u>tremor</u>

* Cognitive symptoms, e.g., fear of dying

* Persistent worry about future <u>panic attacks</u>

* Avoidance of triggering situations





### Diagnostics [[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)




#### Approach




* Consider <u>panic disorder</u> in patients with recurrent <u>panic attacks</u>.

* Perform a complete <u>patient history</u> and <u>physical examination</u>.

* Consider diagnostic studies to rule out organic causes based on clinical evaluation.  [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Confirm the diagnosis using <u>DSM-5</u> criteria.

* Assess for psychiatric and medical comorbidities, e.g., <u>MDD</u>, <u>substance use disorder</u>.

* <u>Evaluate suicide risk</u>.





#### Exclusion of organic causes




Consider the following studies based on clinical suspicion.




* <u>Thyroid function tests</u> to rule out <u>thyroid disease</u>

* <u>CBC</u> to rule out <u>anemia</u>

* <u>ECG</u> to rule out <u>acute coronary syndromes</u>

* <u>Urine drug screen</u> to rule out substance use or <u>poisoning</u>

* <u>BMP</u> to rule out <u>electrolyte</u> disturbances





#### <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria for <u>panic disorder</u> [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)




Diagnosis is confirmed in individuals who meet all of the following criteria.




* Recurrent <u>panic attacks</u>, during which ≥ 4 of the following symptoms occur:

* <u>Tachycardia</u>, <u>palpitations</u>

* Sweating

* Shaking or trembling

* <u>Shortness of breath</u> or sensation of <u>smothering</u>

* Sensation of choking

* <u>Chest pain</u> or discomfort

* Abdominal <u>distress</u> or <u>nausea</u>

* <u>Dizziness</u>, <u>lightheadedness</u>

* Heat sensation or chills

* Parasthesias

* <u>Depersonalization</u> or <u>derealization</u>

* Fear of losing control

* Fear of dying

* ≥ 1 <u>panic attacks</u> followed by ≥ 1 month of one or both of the following:

* Persistent concern about having another <u>panic attack</u> or about its consequences (e.g., losing control)

* Significant maladaptive behavioral changes in response to the attacks (e.g., avoiding situations in which previous attacks occurred)

* <u>Panic attacks</u> are not attributable to:

* Effects of a medication, substance, or medical condition

* Another psychiatric disorder (e.g., <u>specific phobias</u>, <u>social anxiety disorder</u>)





### Differential diagnoses [[18]](/library/r8WfLM0)




* Other anxiety disorders

* <u>GAD</u>

* <u>Substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder</u>

* <u>Anxiety due to another medical condition</u>

* <u>Mood disorders</u>, e.g., <u>MDD</u>, <u>bipolar disorder</u>

* <u>Substance use disorder</u>





### Management [[17]](/library/8FWOPM0)[[18]](/library/r8WfLM0)




See also “<u>Management of acute panic attack</u>.”




> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>panic disorder</u> are at increased risk of <u>suicide</u>. [[9]](/library/R8WlmM0)[[18]](/library/r8WfLM0)




#### General principles




* Treatment options for <u>panic disorder</u> are <u>psychotherapy</u> and/or pharmacotherapy.

* Lifestyle modifications can help reduce symptoms.

* Treatment response is measured using the Panic Disorder Severity Scale.

* Consider indications for specialist referral, e.g., no improvement after first-line treatment.

* Consider hospitalization for patients with intractable symptoms and/or <u>suicidal ideation</u>.





![Panic disorder severity scale (PDSS)](media/d1cd7n9n22i39bcqcorg09lj.jpg)

Panic disorder severity scale (PDSS)




#### <u>Psychotherapy</u> [[17]](/library/8FWOPM0)[[18]](/library/r8WfLM0)




* <u>CBT</u> is the preferred modality.

* Consider especially for patients who decline or do not tolerate pharmacotherapy.

* <u>Effectiveness</u> is similar to pharmacotherapy.





#### Pharmacotherapy




* First-line

* <u>SSRIs</u>, e.g., <u>paroxetine</u> DOSAGE, <u>sertraline</u> DOSAGE

* <u>SNRIs</u>, e.g., <u>venlafaxine</u> DOSAGE

* Additional agents include:

* <u>Benzodiazepines</u>, e.g., <u>alprazolam</u>, <u>clonazepam</u>, or <u>diazepam</u>, for short-term use only

* <u>TCAs</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Cannabis</u> can trigger psychiatric disorders, and there is no scientific evidence to recommend its use in patients with anxiety disorders.




> [!WARNING]
> Long-term use of <u>benzodiazepines</u> is associated with an increased risk of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal. [[18]](/library/r8WfLM0)




#### Indications for referral




Refer to a <u>psychiatrist</u> in any of the following situations.




* There is no improvement with first-line pharmacotherapy.

* The patient does not tolerate pharmacotherapy.

* The patient has comorbid psychiatric and/or <u>substance use disorders</u>.

* Long-term <u>benzodiazepines</u> or alternative agents (e.g., <u>TCAs</u>) are being considered.

---

## Social anxiety disorder

### Definition [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)




<u>Social anxiety disorder</u> is characterized by intense and disproportionate fear and/or anxiety of social situations in which the individual may be scrutinized or judged (e.g., meeting new people, parties, eating in public) that lasts for ≥ 6 months.





### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* One of the most common psychiatric conditions

* 13% lifetime <u>prevalence</u> [[19]](/library/y8Wd6M0)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: <u>adolescence</u> and early adulthood

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2:1)





### Subtypes




* Performance-only social anxiety disorder: : an anxiety disorder characterized by intense fear and/or anxiety related to speaking or performing in public

* Paruresis (<u>shy bladder syndrome</u>): the inability to urinate in the presence of others [[20]](/library/owW0Pn0)





### Clinical features




* Blushing, <u>palpitations</u>, sweating during a social interaction

* Anticipatory anxiety (e.g., worrying weeks in advance about attending a social event)

* Anxiety driven by fear of embarrassment and others noticing the reaction

* Avoidance of fear and/or anxiety triggers (e.g., not attending parties, refusing to attend school)

* In children [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Refusing to speak at social events, crying, throwing a tantrum, clinging to caregiver

* Symptoms occur both in peer settings and with adults.





### Diagnostics [[19]](/library/y8Wd6M0)




#### Approach




* Consider screening individuals with other psychiatric or <u>substance use disorders</u> by asking about:

* Avoidance of social situations or activities

* Feeling anxious or embarrassed in social situations

* Confirm the diagnosis using the <u>DSM-5</u> criteria.

* Assess for comorbidities, e.g., <u>MDD</u>, <u>substance use disorders</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Individuals with <u>social anxiety disorder</u> often do not seek medical care for their psychological symptoms.




#### <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria for <u>social anxiety disorder</u> [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)




Diagnosis is confirmed in individuals who meet all of the following criteria.




* Significant fear or anxiety related to social situations in which scrutiny by others is anticipated (e.g., conversing with or meeting unfamiliar people, eating or giving a speech in front of others)

* Fear of behaving in ways that will lead to negative judgment by others

* Fear or anxiety that is almost always triggered by social situations

* Avoidance of or intense anxiety during social situations

* Fear or anxiety that is disproportionate to the actual threat

* Symptoms that persist for ≥ 6 months

* Symptoms causing significant <u>distress</u> or functional impairment (e.g., social, occupational)

* Symptoms not attributable to or better explained by substance use or another psychiatric or medical condition





### Differential diagnoses [[19]](/library/y8Wd6M0)




* Other anxiety disorders

* <u>Agoraphobia</u>

* <u>Panic disorder</u>

* <u>Generalized anxiety disorder</u>

* <u>Separation anxiety disorder</u>

* Shyness as a <u>personality trait</u>

* Medical conditions that cause embarrassing symptoms (e.g., incontinence, <u>tremor</u>)

* <u>Avoidant personality disorder</u>





### Management [[19]](/library/y8Wd6M0)[[21]](/library/wDahg5)




<u>Psychotherapy</u> and pharmacotherapy can be offered together or alone based on patient preferences and clinical judgment.




* <u>Psychotherapy</u>: : <u>CBT</u> is the most effective type.

* Pharmacotherapy

* <u>Social anxiety disorder</u>

* First-line agents: <u>SSRIs</u>,;  e.g., <u>paroxetine</u> DOSAGE, <u>sertraline</u> DOSAGE or <u>SNRIs</u>, e.g., <u>venlafaxine</u> DOSAGE

* Alternative agents: <u>benzodiazepines</u> (e.g., <u>clonazepam</u>), <u>pregabalin</u>, <u>phenelzine</u>

* <u>Performance-only social anxiety disorder</u>: as needed 30–60 minutes before anxiety-inducing event

* <u>Beta blockers</u>, e.g., <u>propranolol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[19]](/library/y8Wd6M0)

* OR <u>Benzodiazepines</u>, e.g., <u>clonazepam</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>CBT</u> combined with pharmacotherapy provides more rapid and long-lasting improvement of <u>social anxiety disorder</u> than <u>CBT</u> alone. [[19]](/library/y8Wd6M0)

## Specific phobias

* Definition

* Persistent (≥ 6 months) and intense fears of one or more specific situations or objects (phobic stimuli)

* Always occurs during encounters with the phobic stimulus but may already surge in anticipation of an encounter

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Lifetime <u>prevalence</u>: up to 10% of the population [[22]](/library/HGXK0-)

* The average age of onset depends on the <u>specific phobia</u> (e.g., animal <u>phobias</u> more commonly develop in early childhood).

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2:1)

* Common phobias

* Animal: spiders (arachnophobia), insects (entomophobia), dogs (cynophobia)

* Natural environment: heights (acrophobia), storms (astraphobia)

* Blood-injection-injury: blood (hematophobia), needles (belonephobia), dental procedures (odontophobia), fear of injury (traumatophobia)

* Situational: enclosed places (claustrophobia), flying (aviophobia)

* Other: fear of <u>vomiting</u> (emetophobia), the number 13 (triskaidekaphobia), costumed characters (masklophobia), fear of clowns (coulrophobia)

* Treatment

* First-line: <u>CBT</u> with <u>exposure therapy</u>

* Second-line: pharmacotherapy (may be attempted if patients prefer medication to <u>CBT</u> or if <u>CBT</u> is not available) 

* Preferred: <u>benzodiazepines</u>

* Alternative: <u>SSRIs</u> (limited evidence)

* Acute management of needle <u>phobia</u> (blenophobia)  [[23]](/library/lJ1v830)[[24]](/library/zI1r2R0)[[25]](/library/EH18HR0)

* Reassurance

* <u>Topical anesthesia</u>: e.g., <u>eutectic mixture of local anesthetic</u> (<u>EMLA</u>) cream DOSAGE

* Applied tension: repeated flexing of <u>skeletal muscles</u> to prevent <u>vasovagal response</u>

---

## Agoraphobia

* Definition: pronounced fear or anxiety of being in situations that are perceived as difficult to <u>escape</u> from or situations in which it might be difficult to seek help

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2:1)

* Age of onset: < 35 years (60–70% of cases)

* Clinical features

* Fear, anxiety, or even <u>panic attacks</u> over a period of ≥ 6 months in ≥ 2 of the following 5 situations:

* Using public transportation

* Being in open spaces

* Being in enclosed places

* Standing in line or being in a crowd

* Being outside of the home alone

* Active avoidance of these settings unless a companion is present

* Fear can become so severe that the affected individual feels unable to leave the house.

* Some patients can have comorbid <u>panic disorder</u>.

* Treatment

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

* <u>Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors</u>





> [!TIP]
> If a patient meets the criteria for <u>panic disorder</u> and <u>agoraphobia</u>, both conditions should be diagnosed.




References:[[3]](/library/Nta-dm)

---

## Hyperventilation syndrome

### Background [[26]](/library/t8cXoV0)[[27]](/library/F8cgoV0)[[28]](/library/88cOoV0)




* Definition: : a condition characterized by an increase in <u>minute ventilation</u> that exceeds metabolic demands without a clear organic precipitant

* Etiology: : frequently associated with <u>panic disorder</u> and anxiety disorder

* Pathophysiology: <u>hyperventilation</u> → <u>hypocarbia</u> → <u>respiratory alkalosis</u> [[29]](/library/u8cpoV0)





### Clinical features [[30]](/library/Vr1GTR0)



* Cardinal feature: transient <u>hyperventilation</u> 
* Additional symptoms include:

* <u>Dizziness</u>, <u>lightheadedness</u>

* <u>Chest pain</u>, <u>palpitations</u>

* <u>Paresthesias</u> (typically in extremities and/or the perioral area)

* <u>Carpopedal spasm</u>

* Anxiety, sense of impending doom




### Diagnostics [[30]](/library/Vr1GTR0)[[31]](/library/er1xTR0)




<u>Hyperventilation syndrome</u> is a diagnosis of exclusion.




* <u>Pulse oximetry</u>: <u>SpO<sub>2</sub></u> is usually normal.

* <u>Capnography</u> (if available): low <u>EtCO<sub>2</sub></u> initially (normalizes as the episode resolves)

* Tests to rule out an organic cause may include:

* Bedside tests

* <u>POC glucose</u>

* <u>ECG</u>

* <u>Peak expiratory flow</u>

* Laboratory tests

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>BMP</u> (including calculation of <u>anion gap</u>)

* <u>VBG</u> or <u>ABG</u>

* Imaging (as indicated by clinical suspicion), e.g.:

* <u>CXR</u>

* <u>CT angiogram</u> chest

* CT head





### Differential diagnoses




See also “<u>Differential diagnosis of dyspnea</u>.”




* <u>Metabolic acidosis</u> (<u>Kussmaul breathing</u>)

* Diabetic, alcoholic, and/or <u>starvation</u> ketoacidosis

* <u>Lactic acidosis</u> due to <u>salicylate poisoning</u>

* <u>Methanol poisoning</u> or <u>ethylene glycol poisoning</u>

* <u>AKI</u> or advanced <u>CKD</u>

* Cardiac

* <u>Acute coronary syndrome</u>, <u>myocardial infarction</u>

* <u>Congestive heart failure</u>

* Pulmonary

* <u>Pulmonary embolism</u>

* <u>Acute asthma exacerbation</u> or <u>COPD exacerbation</u>

* <u>Emphysema</u> (due to <u>COPD</u>, <u>α1-antitrypsin deficiency</u>)

* <u>Pneumothorax</u>

* <u>Acute respiratory distress syndrome</u> (<u>ARDS</u>)

* Endocrine

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Pheochromocytoma</u>

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Hypocalcemia</u>

* <u>CNS</u> disorders

* <u>Elevated ICP</u>

* <u>Brainstem</u> tumors

* <u>Grand mal seizure</u>

* Other

* Infection (e.g., <u>malaria</u>), <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* <u>Cheyne-Stokes breathing</u>





### Acute management [[30]](/library/Vr1GTR0)




* Exclude <u>immediately life-threatening causes of dyspnea</u>.

* First-line: nonpharmacological treatment

* Offer patient reassurance and if possible, remove stressors.

* Breathing retraining: Focus on diaphragmatic breathing.

* Second-line: short-acting <u>benzodiazepines</u> (e.g., <u>alprazolam</u> DOSAGE) if nonpharmacological interventions fail.

* Interventions to reduce <u>pH</u> directly are typically not necessary.

* See also “<u>Management of acute panic attack</u>” and “<u>Approach to the agitated or violent patient</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Rebreathing into a paper bag can cause significant <u>hypoxemia</u> and is therefore not recommended. [[32]](/library/G8cBLV0)




> [!WARNING]
> Abnormal findings on <u>physical exam</u> (e.g., <u>jugular venous distention</u>, <u>wheezing</u>, <u>crackles</u>, <u>altered mental status</u>) suggest a diagnosis other than <u>hyperventilation syndrome</u>.

## Substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder

* Definition: prominent anxiety or <u>panic attacks</u> within 1 month of use of, or withdrawal from, a substance/medication that is capable of inducing anxiety symptoms [[33]](/library/UHYbpq)

* Etiology [[34]](/library/2HYTpq)[[35]](/library/fHYkpq)

* <u>Alcohol</u>

* <u>Caffeine</u>

* <u>Anticonvulsants</u>, <u>opioids</u>, and sedatives

* <u>Anticholinergics</u>

* <u>Beta agonists</u>

* <u>Corticosteroids</u>

* <u>Amphetamines</u>, <u>cannabis</u>, <u>cocaine</u>, <u>phencyclidine</u>, hallucinogens, and inhalants

* Clinical features [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)[[33]](/library/UHYbpq)[[36]](/library/eHYx6q)

* Fear, anxiety, or <u>panic attacks</u> over a period of 1 month after taking or stopping the substance/medication

* Physical symptoms such as <u>palpitation</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, shaking, <u>shortness of breath</u>, and sweating

* Generalized anxiety or <u>phobia</u> may accompany the substance-induced anxiety

* Treatment

* Discontinuation of the substance/medication

* <u>CBT</u>

* <u>Antidepressants</u> (e.g., <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>SNRIs</u>, <u>TCAs</u>, <u>buspirone</u>)

---

## Anxiety due to another medical condition

Patients should be evaluated for medical conditions that can cause anxiety. <u>Anxiety due to another medical condition</u> is diagnosed if the condition was diagnosed before the onset of anxiety. Possible underlying conditions include:




* Endocrine disorders: e.g., <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>pheochromocytoma</u>, <u>hypoglycemia</u>, hyperadrenalism, <u>hypercortisolism</u>

* Cardiovascular disorders: e.g., <u>congestive heart failure</u>, <u>pulmonary embolism</u>, <u>arrhythmia</u> (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation</u>)

* Respiratory disorders: e.g., <u>asthma</u>, <u>COPD</u>, <u>pneumonia</u>

* Infectious diseases: e.g., <u>epiglottitis</u>

* Metabolic disorders: e.g., <u>porphyria</u>, <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>

* Neurological disorders: e.g., <u>neoplasm</u>, vestibular dysfunction, <u>encephalitis</u>, <u>seizure disorders</u>

* Gynecological disorders: e.g., <u>genito-pelvic penetration disorder</u>, <u>hydatidiform mole</u>

* Other: e.g., <u>menopause</u>, <u>insomnia</u>, <u>fibromyalgia</u>, <u>schizophrenia</u>, <u>gender dysphoria</u>

---

## Separation anxiety disorder

* Description: a disorder characterized by excessive fear, anxiety, or avoidance of separation from major attachment figures

* <u>Separation anxiety disorder</u> differs from nonpathological <u>separation anxiety</u> in its intensity and effect on the social and academic life of the individual.

* <u>Separation anxiety</u> is normal in children under a developmental age of 3 years. [[37]](/library/Pr1WhR0)

* Typically develops after a stressful life event, usually involving some form of loss (e.g., <u>death</u> of a relative, parental divorce, change of school)

* Onset: the condition can occur in, or persist into, adulthood and may have a debilitating effect on an individual's ability to work or socialize in the absence of attachment figures.

* Diagnostic criteria (<u>DSM-V</u>) [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Fear of separation from major attachment figures, that is excessive for developmental level, involving at least 3 of the following features:

* Recurrent and excessive <u>distress</u> prior to, or during, separation

* Persistent worrying about the loss of attachment figures (e.g., due to illness, injury, or <u>death</u>)

* Persistent worrying about separation due to the individual being lost, kidnapped, injured, or ill

* Persistent reluctant to leave home due to fear of separation

* Avoidance of being left alone (e.g., at home or elsewhere)

* Avoidance of falling asleep, or sleeping away from home, without major attachment figure

* Persistent nightmares about separation

* Persistent somatic symptoms (e.g., <u>headaches</u>, <u>nausea</u>/<u>vomiting</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>)

* Duration: symptoms persist for at least 4 weeks in children/<u>adolescents</u> and 6 months in adults

* Significant impairment of academic, social, and/or work life (e.g., often a precursor to school refusal)

* Symptoms are not attributable to another psychiatric disorder (e.g., <u>autism spectrum disorder</u>, <u>psychosis</u>, other anxiety disorders).

* Treatment of separation anxiety disorder [[38]](/library/4E13Di0)

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>

* All age groups: <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> (e.g., <u>exposure therapy</u>)

* Children: <u>family therapy</u> and parent-child interaction therapy

* Pharmacotherapy: <u>SSRIs</u> (e.g., <u>fluoxetine</u>) indicated as an adjunct to <u>psychotherapy</u> if there is moderate to severe functional impairment

* Complications

* Children: academic and social consequences of school refusal

* Adults: <u>depression</u> and <u>panic disorder</u> [[37]](/library/Pr1WhR0)





> [!TIP]
> Children under 3 years of age commonly undergo periods of <u>separation anxiety</u> from attachment figures as a normal part of their development. The diagnosis of <u>separation anxiety disorder</u> should only be considered if the symptoms become excessive for developmental level. [[37]](/library/Pr1WhR0)

---

## Selective mutism

* Description: a psychiatric disorder characterized by the inability to speak in specific social situations (e.g., during class) 

* Typically normal development of language and speech.

* Onset: generally before 5 years of age, although may not become clinically relevant until the child is required to perform verbally (e.g., with the start of school)

* Diagnostic criteria (<u>DSM-V</u>) [[3]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Consistent inability to speak in specific social settings where speaking is expected (e.g., does not speak in class but speaks at home)

* Interferes with academic or professional performance and social interaction

* Duration of symptoms: at least 1 month

* The inability to speak is not due to difficulties or discomfort with the spoken language expected in the social situation.

* The inability to speak is not attributable to <u>schizophrenia spectrum disorder</u> or another <u>psychotic disorder</u>, <u>autism spectrum disorder</u>, or a communication disorder.

* Treatment [[39]](/library/QrYuSq)

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u> (e.g., <u>exposure therapy</u>) at all ages

* Children: <u>family therapy</u> and parent-child interaction therapy

* Pharmacotherapy: <u>SSRIs</u> (e.g., <u>fluoxetine</u>) may be beneficial in those who do not respond to <u>psychotherapy</u>

* Complications: may coexist with <u>social anxiety disorder</u> and may also result in school refusal

---
